| `files` | strings | artifacts | the files it consists of, from the project root; the files in its attachments/ count too |  |
| `madeFrom` | object | artifacts | recorded on delivery, never by hand: the commit it was made at (commit), one sha256 digest over its inputs and the data of the items it uses (inputs), and the moment (at) |  |
| `deliveredOn` | date | artifacts | the day it was delivered, recorded on delivery: the diary tells it on that day |  |

**Link relations** — only the direction written is stored; the inverse is derived when read.

| Relation | Inverse | Reads as |
|---|---|---|
| `satisfies` | `satisfied-by` | delivers or proves the requirement |
| `satisfied-by` | `satisfies` | is delivered by |
| `specified-by` | `specifies` | follows the specification |
| `specifies` | `specified-by` | is the specification followed by |
| `supersedes` | `superseded-by` | replaces an earlier version, decision or artifact |
| `superseded-by` | `supersedes` | is replaced by |
| `settles` | `settled-by` | is the decision that answers |
| `settled-by` | `settles` | is answered by the decision |
| `records` | `recorded-by` | is the session recording a sitting of |
| `recorded-by` | `records` | has a sitting recorded by the session |
| `produces` | `produced-by` | is the work that makes the artifact |
| `produced-by` | `produces` | is made by |
| `uses` | `used-by` | is made from the data of: a test, a property, another artifact |
| `used-by` | `uses` | has its data used by the artifact |

**Checks**, run by `naima check`

| Check | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `requirements-proven` | a requirement marked met has a proof that passed and none that refutes it; one proven but still stated is noted; one that nothing satisfies or verifies is noted; one proposed by someone other than the owner and never confirmed is noted |
| `specs-versioned` | one version of a specification is current; a version superseded by a current one is marked superseded; a spec supersedes only an earlier version of itself; an open item following a superseded version is noted |
| `decisions-settled` | an open item waiting on the owner's decision (runBy human, humanBecause decision) that a settled decision settles is noted, to be acted on rather than asked; a decision superseded by a settled one is marked superseded |
| `release-stages` | a release marked released has every stage recorded or skipped with who decided; one hand-edited past the hook is a problem |
| `artifacts-current` | as notes: an artifact past its due day and not delivered; a delivered artifact whose inputs, or the data of the items it uses, changed since it was made; a planned artifact nothing produces |
| `model-first` | a change triaged as having states or concurrency (stateful: true) that landed (fixedOn set) with no models or properties item linked to it, and no waiver of this check filed with its reason, is noted, as the project's setting (planning option modelFirst) says: strict notes every one; advisory notes a new protocol or concurrency as a must, other new behaviour as advice, and nothing on existing code; deferred notes the deferral and its planned todo instead of each change |

**Views**, printed by `naima view <name>`

| View | What it shows |
|---|---|
| `requirements` | every requirement that is not dropped: its status, whether it is proven, what satisfies it and what proves it |
| `releases` | every release in progress or done: its status and which stages it still owes |

**Summary sections**: `model-first`.

**Write hooks**, run on every item write

| Hook | What it does |
|---|---|
| `planning-stamps` | a new spec takes its name and version from its title (`Export format v2` is export-format, version 2) unless given; a new decision is dated today unless given |
| `requirements-confirmed` | a new requirement whose origin says someone other than the owner asked for it is proposed, not stated; it becomes stated or met only through naima confirm, with the owner's words restated, or is dropped; --force takes a move on |
| `release-stages` | a release is marked released only once every stage is recorded, or skipped and said by whom |
| `artifacts-delivered` | an artifact becomes delivered only with its files — every path in files exists, and there is at least one, there or in its attachments — and is then stamped with madeFrom (the commit, the digest over its inputs and the data of what it uses, the moment) and deliveredOn; any other write that changes those two is refused |

**Setup**, put in place by `naima init` and `naima update` where missing

| Step | What it puts in place |
|---|---|
| `model-first-setting` | at init, when the project has not chosen how strictly it applies model first and has no items yet: write init's proposal (strict for a new project, advisory when the repository already holds substantial code) and say the question to put to the owner, who may keep it, change it or defer it |

**Shipped rules**, active in every project that loads the plugin, listed by `naima rules`

| Rule | Title | For | Strength | Enforced by | Verified by | Ack |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `requirements-elicited-at-every-prompt` | Requirements are elicited at every prompt, each with how it is checked or measured | agents | must | `requirements-proven` | `requirements-proven` | `Elicitation mode on` |
| `behaviour-designed-from-a-model` | Behaviour with states or concurrency is modelled and verified before it is coded | everyone | must | `model-first` | `model-first` | `Model first mode on` |

## knowledge

Knowledge entries: facts, hypotheses, findings and lessons, each with its basis — a source, evidence, or other entries — and its kind.

Its contributions' qualified ids are `knowledge/<name>`.

A project's lasting knowledge as items: what is known, and on what basis. A **knowledge entry** (`naima new knowledge`) is one statement. Its `basis` says why it is believed: `given` — known without investigation, a premise named by its `givenBy` (the owner, a datasheet, a contract), which starts `established` and can still be `retracted`; `evidence` — established by experiments, analyses, tests or proofs, which starts as a `hypothesis` and carries its falsifier on its page; `derived` — following from other entries, linked `derives-from`. Evidence is any item — a test, an analysis, an artifact, a property — linked `supports` or `contradicts` the entry; it counts only once it succeeded: a status that proves (a passed test, a property that holds) or that its type marks positive (a confirmed analysis). An artifact never counts: it is material, linked `relates-to`, and an entry whose only support is an artifact is a problem. Its `kind` says what sort of statement it is: built in, `fact`, `hypothesis`, `finding` and `lesson` (what experience taught, whose page holds What happened, The lesson and How to apply it); a project declares its own kinds, each with the sections and fields its entries require, under this plugin's `kinds` option. A kind adds requirements, never statuses. A lesson is **codified** once a rule, a test or a property that holds it links `codifies` to it: `naima show` lists it as `codified-by`, and `naima knowledge` says it. `naima check` fails on an established entry with nothing passing behind it (or a given one that names no `givenBy`) and on an entry missing what its kind requires; it notes an entry both supported and refuted by current evidence, one derived from a refuted or retracted entry, and, with the `lessonsCodified` option, an established lesson nothing codifies. `naima knowledge` prints the established entries by kind, each with its source or evidence.

Options, each with the default it takes when nothing sets it:

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `kinds` | `{} (the built-in fact, hypothesis, finding, lesson)` | the project's own kinds of entry, by name: `says`, and the `sections` and `fields` its entries require, such as { "incident": { "says": "something that went wrong in production", "sections": ["Timeline"] } }; a built-in kind named here gains the requirements |
| `lessonsCodified` | `false` | true to note an established lesson that no rule, test or property codifies |

**Uses**, declared by other plugins: fields `kind`.

### naima knowledge

Print the established knowledge entries by kind, each with its source or evidence.

**Enforces**: Nothing: it reads the knowledge entries and prints them; `naima check` holds what an entry must stand on.

```sh
naima knowledge [--kind <k>] [--all]
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--kind` |  | only the entries of this kind |
| `--all` |  | every entry, whatever its status: hypotheses, refuted, retracted and superseded ones too |

Examples:

```sh
naima knowledge
naima knowledge --kind lesson
naima knowledge --all
```

### type: knowledge

Knowledge: one statement the project knows, or is finding out, with its basis — given by a source, established by evidence, or derived from other entries — and its kind. Items live in `naima-tracker/naima-data/knowledge/`; a new one starts as `hypothesis`.

| Status | Category | Flags | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hypothesis` | open |  | under investigation: the evidence is not in yet |
| `established` | done |  | holds: given by its source, supported by passing evidence, or derived from established entries |
| `refuted` | done |  | the evidence went against it; kept as history |
| `inconclusive` | open |  | investigated, and the evidence settles nothing yet |
| `retracted` | done |  | a given that no longer holds |
| `superseded` | done |  | replaced by a later entry, linked `supersedes` when the planning plugin is loaded |

**Fields**

| Field | Kind | Applies to | Meaning | Values |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `basis` | enum | knowledge | why the entry is believed | `given` known without investigation: a premise, named by its `givenBy`; a given entry starts established; `evidence` established by experiments, analyses, tests or proofs linked `supports`; an evidence entry starts as a hypothesis; `derived` follows from other entries, linked `derives-from` |
| `givenBy` | string | knowledge | who or what gives a given entry: the owner, a datasheet, a contract |  |

**Link relations** — only the direction written is stored; the inverse is derived when read.

| Relation | Inverse | Reads as |
|---|---|---|
| `supports` | `supported-by` | is evidence for the knowledge entry |
| `supported-by` | `supports` | is supported by the evidence |
| `contradicts` | `contradicted-by` | is evidence against the knowledge entry: it refutes it |
| `contradicted-by` | `contradicts` | is refuted by the evidence |
| `derives-from` | `derived-into` | follows from the knowledge entry |
| `derived-into` | `derives-from` | is a premise of the knowledge entry |
| `codifies` | `codified-by` | holds the lesson from now on: a rule, a test or a property |
| `codified-by` | `codifies` | is held from now on by the rule, test or property |

**Checks**, run by `naima check`

| Check | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `knowledge-basis` | an established entry stands on its basis: a given one names its source, one on evidence has evidence that succeeded linked `supports` (a passed test, a property that holds, a confirmed analysis), never an artifact alone; an entry both supported and refuted by current evidence, or derived from a refuted or retracted one, is noted |
| `knowledge-kinds` | an entry of a kind carries the sections and fields its kind requires; a kind not declared is noted |

**Extensions** of other plugins' types and fields

- field `kind`: values `fact` a knowledge entry: a statement about the world taken as true: given by a source, or established; `hypothesis` a knowledge entry: a statement under investigation, with what would refute it; `finding` a knowledge entry: what an investigation found: established, or refuted, by its evidence; `lesson` a knowledge entry: what experience taught: what happened, the lesson, how to apply it; codified once a rule or a check holds it

**Write hooks**, run on every item write

| Hook | What it does |
|---|---|
| `knowledge-starts-by-basis` | a new knowledge entry whose basis is given starts established; any other starts as a hypothesis |

## roles

The roles of the company of agents as data: what each owns and refuses, and the kinds of work on its queue.

Its contributions' qualified ids are `roles/<name>`.

A role is what it refuses: each one says what it owns and what it will not do, so no one marks their own homework. The roles are data — by default the thirteen of the company of agents (docs/purpose.md), and `plugins.roles.options.roles` adds a project's own or replaces one by name — and any plugin may contribute one to the `roles` point. Every kind a role takes is a value of the trackers' `kind` field, so the kinds are one vocabulary and a kind no role takes is a note. An item is on a role's queue by its `role` field when set, else by its `kind` or its type; `naima roles` lists the roles with their open counts, and `naima queue --role <role>` lists one's queue, most urgent first.

Options, each with the default it takes when nothing sets it:

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `roles` | `{}` | role name → { "title", "owns", "refuses": [...], "kinds": [...], "types": [...] }: adds a role, or replaces the default one of that name. refuses is never empty. |

**Extension points** it declares: `roles`.

**Uses**, declared by other plugins: fields `kind`.

### naima roles

Every role: what it owns, what it refuses, the kinds and types on its queue, and how many open items are on it.

**Enforces**: Nothing: it only reads; a role that refuses nothing is refused when the plugin loads.

```sh
naima roles [--json]
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--json` |  | print the roles as JSON: name, title, owns, refuses, kinds, types, flow, open |

Examples:

```sh
naima roles
naima roles --json
```

**Fields**

| Field | Kind | Applies to | Meaning | Values |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `role` | enum | every type | the role whose queue the item is on, when its kind or type does not say: any role a loaded plugin contributes | the name of any contribution to `roles`; one, or a list of several |

**Extensions** of other plugins' types and fields

- field `kind`: values `decision` work on the owner's queue; `coordination` work on the coordinator's queue; `review` work on the lead developer's queue; `design` work on the lead developer's queue; `research` work on the lead developer's queue; `code` work on the implementer's queue; `refactor` work on the implementer's queue; `test` work on the tester's queue; `evidence` work on the evidence owner's queue; `report` work on the filer's queue; `triage` work on the filer's queue; `model` work on the verification engineer's queue; `verification` work on the verification engineer's queue; `release` work on the release manager's queue; `writing` work on the documentarian's queue; `docs` work on the documentarian's queue; `announcement` work on the announcer's queue; `community` work on the community steward's queue; `business` work on the business's queue; `site` work on the website manager's queue

**Roles**, listed by `naima roles`; `naima queue --role <role>` shows one's queue

| Role | Title | Owns | Refuses | Queue: kinds and types |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `owner` | Owner | the decisions: judgement, a reserved decision, a credential, a physical act | any machine work; being asked what an agent can find out | `decision`, every `decisions` |
| `coordinator` | Coordinator | the conversation with the owner; the trunk, as its single writer: it alone lands, pushes it, publishes the site and makes releases; the timer, spawning and merging workers | work a worker could do; more than one question at a time | `coordination` |
| `lead-developer` | Lead developer | the queue: ranking it, sweeping fixed-but-unproven items, preparing branches, the merge train | merging without the gates; closing an item on reasoning; closing its own branch's items | `review`, `design`, `research` |
| `implementer` | Implementer | one item, one cause, one branch: the code, analysis or text it asks for | widening scope; spawning workers; touching the trunk | `code`, `refactor` |
| `tester` | Tester | performing gestures on the running software and writing down what happened | fixing what it finds; testing what it just wrote | `test`, every `tests` |
| `evidence-owner` | Evidence owner | whether a gesture proves the claim, weighed by the evidence ranking and red-then-green | performing the gesture it then judges; accepting inspection as proof | `evidence` |
| `filer` | Filer | classification, triage fields, reports routed to the right tracker | inventing scope; deciding whether something is proven | `report`, `triage` |
| `verification-engineer` | Verification engineer | the formal models and properties, and running their verifiers | changing a model to make a property hold; calling a property proven past its expiry | `model`, `verification`, every `properties` |
| `release-manager` | Release manager | opening a release item, running its stages in order, recording each stage's output | releasing off a gate that does not hold; deciding to release; judging whether the code is good enough | `release`, every `releases` |
| `documentarian` | Documentarian | the words: docs pages with the feature, the changelog, the documentation map | documenting what does not exist in the code; deciding whether to announce | `writing`, `docs` |
| `announcer` | Announcer | release notes, changelog entries, site and README copy, announcements | announcing a feature that is not announceable: user-facing, shipped, documented and checked by a person or end to end; deciding when to announce | `announcement` |
| `community-steward` | Community steward | turning outside issues and pull requests into items, and keeping the link back | merging anything; promising a contributor an outcome | `community` |
| `business` | Business | researching licence, funding, sponsorship, citation and adoption options, filed as decisions | acting on any of it before the owner decides; committing the project to anything | `business` |

## announce

Announceability, computed: a feature may be announced only once user-facing, shipped, documented and checked by a person or end to end.

Its contributions' qualified ids are `announce/<name>`.

What may be announced is computed, never declared. A feature is **announceable** when it is user-facing (`facing: user`), shipped (a status in `shippedStatuses`, or closed into the archive), documented (its `docs` field names a page) and checked: a passed item verifies it whose `runBy` is in `checkedBy` — a person, or an agent driving the running software, end to end — or whose `evidenceKind` is in `checkedEvidence`. A refuting proof outweighs any that proves. `naima announce` lists the announceable features, major ones (`major: true`) first, since a date or on a gate: the only source of release notes, changelog entries and announcements. With `--all` it adds every user-facing feature that is not announceable, with what it lacks. `naima credits` prints the standard credit of everything the project uses from outside — Naima itself, the plugins and stances it loads from elsewhere, what a plugin runs without installing it, the tools the loaded plugins declare — each with where it is published (homepage and source), its authors, its licence and the version used; `--markdown` prints it as the Credits section that `naima announce --gate` and `naima changes` end the release notes with. This is provisional. The check `copy-names-only-announceable` fails when a file of the `copy` option names, by its label or its full title, a feature that is not announceable, so the README and the site never promise what is not true.

Options, each with the default it takes when nothing sets it:

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `featureTypes` | `["features"]` | item types whose items are features |
| `shippedStatuses` | `["shipped"]` | statuses in which a feature is shipped |
| `checkedBy` | `["human", "agent-hands"]` | values of a proof's `runBy` that count as checked: by a person, or end to end on the running software |
| `checkedEvidence` | `["owner-gesture"]` | values of a proof's `evidenceKind` that count as checked, whoever ran it |
| `copy` | `["README.md"]` | files, from the project root, of public copy that may name only announceable features; one missing is skipped |

**Uses**, declared by other plugins: types `features`; fields `docs`, `runBy`, `fixedOn`; relations `verified-by`.

### naima announce

The features that may be announced — user-facing, shipped, documented and checked by a person or end to end — major first: the source of release notes.

**Enforces**: Nothing: it only lists, and only features user-facing, shipped, documented and checked by a person or end to end.

```sh
naima announce [--since <date>] [--gate <gate>] [--all] [--json]
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--since` |  | only features shipped (fixedOn) on or after the date, YYYY-MM-DD |
| `--gate` |  | only features on that gate: what a release off it announces |
| `--all` |  | also every user-facing feature that is not announceable, with what it lacks |
| `--json` |  | print each feature as JSON: item, title, major, shippedOn, announceable, lacks, checkedBy |

Examples:

```sh
naima announce
naima announce --since 2026-09-01
naima announce --gate v1 --all
naima announce --json
```

### naima credits

Every attribution in use in the project — Naima itself, each plugin or stance loaded from outside Naima, what a plugin runs without installing it, and every tool a loaded plugin declares — each with its name, homepage, source, authors, licence and version, and what it fails to declare (provisional).

**Enforces**: Nothing: it only prints.

```sh
naima credits [--json
naima --markdown]
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--json` |  | print each credit as JSON: name, homepage, source, authors, license, version, kind, plugin, missing |
| `--markdown` |  | print the credits as the Credits section of release notes, in Markdown |

Examples:

```sh
naima credits
naima credits --json
naima credits --markdown
```

**Fields**

| Field | Kind | Applies to | Meaning | Values |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `facing` | enum | features, any type tagged `archive` | whom the feature is for: only a user-facing one is ever announced | `user` someone using the software sees it; `internal` only who works on the software sees it |
| `major` | boolean | features, any type tagged `archive` | a feature an announcement leads with |  |

**Checks**, run by `naima check`

| Check | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `copy-names-only-announceable` | the project's public copy (the copy option: README.md by default) names no feature, by its label or its title, that is not announceable |

## loop

The non-stop loop: work on an explicit target until only the owner's work is left, then hand him the ordered list.

Its contributions' qualified ids are `loop/<name>`.

`naima loop <target>` is what an agent runs on every tick of its wake-up timer. The target is chosen before starting: a work list — an item whose README lists steps as `- [ ]` and `- [x]` lines, a step that waits carrying `deferred: <why>` — an epic, or a gate. The loop stops when what is left needs only the owner: a work list when every line is done or deferred; an epic or a gate when every open item is a reserved decision (`humanBecause: decision`) or a proof only a person or a build can give (`runBy: human`, `runBy: build`). Once stopped it prints the owner's actions in order — decisions first, then credentials, physical acts, judgements and builds — each saying why it is his, and the proving gestures nobody has run yet, to try while he is away. The timer is the agent harness's; the plugin states its cadence, `every` minutes.

Options, each with the default it takes when nothing sets it:

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `every` | `3` | the wake-up cadence the loop states, in whole minutes; `--every` overrides it for one run |

**Uses**, declared by other plugins: fields `runBy`, `humanBecause`, `fixedOn`; relations `has-part`, `verified-by`.

### naima loop

The non-stop loop on a target chosen before starting — a work list, an epic or a gate: done or not, the next agent work, the stop verdict, and once stopped the owner's ordered action list, each line saying why it is his.

**Enforces**: The loop runs only on a target chosen before starting — a work list, an epic or a gate —; with --check, exit 1 while it is not stopped.

```sh
naima loop <target> [--every <minutes>] [--json] [--check]
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--every` |  | the wake-up cadence in minutes, for this run; default the plugin's option every (3) |
| `--json` |  | print the verdict as JSON: target, kind, title, every, done, total, left, stopped, verdict, next, owner, untried, tick |
| `--check` |  | exit 1 while the loop is not stopped |

Examples:

```sh
naima loop todos/tonight
naima loop epics/onboarding --json
naima loop beta --check
```

## beta-markers

Markers in the code for behaviour shipped without proof.

Its contributions' qualified ids are `beta-markers/<name>`.

A marker is a comment in the project's own source naming the item whose passing would prove the marked behaviour: `// naima:beta tests/export-keeps-alpha  export of layered files is unproven`. Always on: it scans every source file of the project, so a marker anywhere is held without listing where to look. A marker names its item as any item reference; a `type/slug` written before the item was archived still finds it in the archive. A marker is wrong in two ways: it names nothing (dangling, said with why), or it outlives its proof — the item it names has passed or is no longer open (stale). Both fail `naima check`: a stale marker teaches readers that markers mean nothing.

Options, each with the default it takes when nothing sets it:

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `paths` | `every file git tracks or would track (outside git, every file under the root but hidden directories, node_modules, dist and build)` | files or directories, from the project root, to scan instead of the whole project |
| `extensions` | `[".ts", ".tsx", ".js", ".mjs", ".py", ".rs", ".go", ".java", ".c", ".h"]` | file extensions to scan |
| `pattern` | `a comment (//, #, --, ;, *) followed by naima:beta <ref> <what>` | a regular expression with named groups ref and what, matched against each line |

**Uses**, declared by other plugins: fields `closedFrom`.

### naima beta

List what is marked as shipped without proof, and the state of each proof.

**Enforces**: Nothing: it only reads.

```sh
naima beta [--check]
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--check` |  | exit 1 when a marker is stale or dangling |

Examples:

```sh
naima beta
naima beta --check
```

**Checks**, run by `naima check`

| Check | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `beta-markers` | every marker names an open item; none outlives its proof |

**Summary sections**: `shipped without proof`.

## verifier

Properties checked by formal-methods tools, with each run attached as evidence.

Its contributions' qualified ids are `verifier/<name>`.

A `properties` item names a `verifier` (an adapter any plugin can contribute), a `model` file (a path from the project root) and a `property` in the verifier's own language. `naima verify` runs the adapter and attaches the run — verdict, output, the adapter's `details` of how it reached the verdict when it gives them, the model's sha256, and one digest over every file the run read (the model and what the adapter's `inputs` says it includes) and the tool's version (the adapter's `version`) — and the counterexample as its own file, then sets the status from the verdict. Every file is hashed by the content git commits: a text file's CRLF line endings are read as LF, so a run made on a Windows checkout with core.autocrlf is current on any other. `--tool-args=<flags>` passes the tool flags the adapter declares in `toolArgs` as changing what it prints, never the verdict, and keeps them with the run, outside its identity. `--host <host>` runs the verifier in the checkout of a host the long-work plugin declares, through that host's Naima (`naima verify --emit`, which prints the run and writes nothing), and attaches the run here, marked with the host, only when it was made on exactly what this checkout has. A conclusive run (holds or violated) already recorded on the property with the same identity — verifier, model, property, `verifierOptions`, and the one digest over every input and the tool's version — is reused instead of repeated: `naima verify` says `reused` and names the run, and `--force "<reason>"` runs it again, keeping the reason with the new run. An error is never reused. Every run is kept, two made in the same instant included. A property that holds is evidence exactly as a passed test is: it can `verify` a bug and close it. A verdict is only as good as what it was reached on, so `naima check` fails when a property claims to hold and its property, verifier, model path, `verifierOptions`, model contents, any file it includes, the set of files it reads, or the tool's version have changed since the run. A property that holds and proves a change — it verifies or satisfies a bug, a todo or a feature — is expected to carry a violated run of the same property, with its counterexample, on other inputs (`property-failed-first`), and to be backed by a witness property that holds, linked by `witnesses` (`property-witnessed`); both are notes that name the property, so either can be waived with its reason. A `models` item marks a model, by its path in `model`, as in development: while it is, the staleness of its properties is a note rather than a problem and the two change checks ask nothing of them; it leaves development (status `stable`) only when every property verified on it holds on a run of exactly what it has now. When the project has a `models` item, `naima summary`, `naima hello` and `naima guide` say once, in one line, that the code of a state machine can be generated from a model with naima-codegen (https://github.com/naima-project/naima-codegen), checked against it. A refactoring of a model is proved by equivalence: `naima equivalent <model>` finds, in git, the earlier version each property's last run read, has the verifier compare it with the model as it is now modulo an equivalence (`--modulo`, the adapter's first by default), and, when the two are equivalent, records for each property a run that carries the earlier verdict over to the new version, marked `carried` with the run it came from, the earlier version's sha256 and the comparison's output; a later `naima verify` reuses it. Nothing carries over when the versions differ, when the equivalence does not preserve the property, or when anything besides the model changed — the property, its options, another input, the tool's version. The shipped adapters are `example-regex`, a stand-in that shows the shape of a real one, and `naima-codegen`, which runs naima-codegen's checks on a codegen project: its `model` is the project's `codegen.toml`, the project its directory (or the one above, for `model/codegen.toml`) unless `verifierOptions.project` names it; `property` `refines` runs `naima-codegen check-refinement` (with `--no-model` when `verifierOptions.noModel` is true), which holds when every check of the generated machine against the model holds and is violated, the failing checks its counterexample, when one fails; `properties` runs `check-refinement --properties`, every property item of the codegen project on the refined systems, and the path of one of their `.mcf` files, the same run judged on that property alone; `verifierOptions.group`, a group or a list, limits the run to those groups, and `timeoutSeconds` ends it as unknown. A project naima-codegen refuses is an error run whose output begins `refused:`. Every file of the codegen project — model, policy, `codegen.toml`, properties, generated code — is an input, so a regeneration makes its runs stale; the version is the first line of `naima-codegen --version`, or, for a naima-codegen without one, the commit of the git checkout the program runs from, said to be the pinned commit (`5aca11dbb1e0`, whose git object id is its checksum) or not. naima-codegen is found on PATH and is not installed by `naima tools`: missing, the run is an error whose output begins `tool missing:` and says how to install it from its repository at the pinned commit; the launcher lets `naima verify`, and no other command, start it. The opt-in `verifier-mcrl2` plugin contributes the mCRL2 adapter.

**Extension points** it declares: `verifiers`.

### naima verify

Run the verifier of properties and attach each run as evidence, here or in a declared host's checkout.

**Enforces**: A property holds only with a run of its verifier on exactly what it has now, attached as evidence; every input is hashed by its committed content, a text file's CRLF line endings read as LF, so every checkout hashes alike; a model or input outside the project is refused; a conclusive run (holds or violated) already recorded on the same identity — every input's digest with the tool's version, and the options — is reused, not repeated, unless --force gives the reason to run it again; --tool-args passes only flags the verifier declares as leaving the verdict alone, recorded with the run; with --host, the run is made in the host's checkout, which writes nothing there, and kept here only when it was made on exactly what this checkout has.

**Progress**: The properties done of those asked, with a rate and an ETA; within a property, each stage of its verifier with the count its tool exposes — for mCRL2 each tool, with the states lps2lts explores and the BES equations pbessolve generates; with --host, the host's own progress lines, as notes.

```sh
naima verify <property>...
naima verify --all [--force "<reason>"] [--tool-args="<flags>"] [--host <host>] [--emit]
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--all` |  | every property item |
| `--force` |  | run again even when a run of the same identity is recorded, for the reason given: kept with the new run |
| `--tool-args` |  | flags for the tool, given with = since they start with a dash (--tool-args=--timings), separated by spaces, each one the verifier declares as changing what the tool prints, never the verdict (for mCRL2 --verbose and --timings): kept with the run, and not part of its identity |
| `--host` |  | run the verifier in the checkout of this host, declared in the long-work plugin's hosts option, through the host's own Naima over ssh; the run comes back and is attached here, refused when the host's checkout differs from this one |
| `--emit` |  | print each run as one JSON line and write nothing: what --host asks the host's Naima |

Examples:

```sh
naima verify no-deadlock
naima verify --all
naima verify no-deadlock --force "the first run was cut short by a reboot"
naima verify no-deadlock --host lab --tool-args="--verbose --timings"
```

### naima verifiers

List the verifier adapters every plugin contributes.

**Enforces**: Nothing: it only reads.

```sh
naima verifiers
```

Examples:

```sh
naima verifiers
```

### naima equivalent

Compare a model with the earlier version its properties were verified on, modulo an equivalence, and carry each result over to the model as it is now when the two are equivalent: a refactoring proved without running its properties again.

**Enforces**: A result carries over only from a conclusive run on an earlier version of the model, with everything else it read unchanged — the property, the options, every other input, the tool's version — when the verifier finds the two versions equivalent and says the equivalence preserves the property; the carried run is recorded as such, naming the run it came from, the earlier version and the comparison.

**Progress**: The stages of the comparison, each tool with the count it exposes — for mCRL2 the states lps2lts explores, for the earlier version and then for the model as it is now.

```sh
naima equivalent <model> [--modulo <equivalence>] [--from <revision>]
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--modulo` |  | the equivalence to compare modulo, one the verifier names; absent, its first, the strongest |
| `--from` |  | the git revision holding the earlier version; absent, the version each run read is looked for in the index and in the commits that changed the model |

Examples:

```sh
naima equivalent models/scheduler.mcrl2
naima equivalent models/scheduler.mcrl2 --modulo dpbranching-bisim --from main
```

### type: properties

Properties: a property of the software, proven or refuted by a verifier. Items live in `naima-tracker/naima-data/properties/`; a new one starts as `open`.

| Status | Category | Flags | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `open` | open |  | not yet verified |
| `holds` | done | proves | the last run on the current model holds |
| `violated` | open | refutes | the last run found a counterexample |
| `error` | open |  | the last run could not reach a verdict |

### type: models

Models: a model, or another artifact properties are verified on, named by its path in model: whether it is in development. Items live in `naima-tracker/naima-data/models/`; a new one starts as `development`.

| Status | Category | Flags | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `development` | open |  | changed across several landings: its properties' results are informational, their staleness a note, and the change checks ask nothing of them |
| `stable` | done |  | out of development: every property of the model held on a run of what it had when it left |

**Fields**

| Field | Kind | Applies to | Meaning | Values |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `verifier` | string | properties | the adapter that checks it |  |
| `model` | string | properties, models | the model or specification file, from the project root, and inside it |  |
| `property` | string | properties | the property, in the verifier's own language |  |
| `lastRun` | string | properties | the attachment holding the last run: a file name in the item's attachments/ |  |
| `verifierOptions` | object | properties | options handed to the verifier with the model and the property, as a JSON object |  |

**Link relations** — only the direction written is stored; the inverse is derived when read.

| Relation | Inverse | Reads as |
|---|---|---|
| `witnesses` | `witnessed-by` | is a witness property, showing that the behaviour is reachable, for |
| `witnessed-by` | `witnesses` | is backed by the witness property |

**Checks**, run by `naima check`

| Check | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `property-evidence` | a property names a known verifier and an existing model; one that holds carries a run of its current property, verifier, model and options, on every file it reads as it is now and the tool's version as it is now |
| `property-failed-first` | a property that holds and proves a change — it verifies or satisfies a bug, a todo or a feature — also carries a violated run of the same property, with its counterexample, on other inputs than those it holds on: the model before the change. A note, naming the property as its subject, so it can be waived with a reason |
| `property-witnessed` | a property that holds and proves a change is backed by a witness property that holds — one linked to it by witnesses, showing the new behaviour is reachable, so the property does not hold only because the situation never arises. A note, naming the property as its subject, so it can be waived with a reason; a witnesses link with an item that is not a property at either end is noted too |
| `model-development` | every models item names one model, and no two name the same; a stable model whose property does not hold on a run of what it has now is noted, since it either needs verifying or is in development again |

**Summary sections**: `codegen`.

**Guide sections**, printed first by `naima guide`

| Section | What it shows |
|---|---|
| `codegen` | when the project has a models item, one line: the code can be generated from the model with naima-codegen |

**Write hooks**, run on every item write

| Hook | What it does |
|---|---|
| `property-reopens-when-changed` | changing a property's property, model, verifier or verifierOptions sets its status back to open: the last run was reached on something else, and says nothing about it |
| `holds-only-by-verify` | a property becomes holds only with a run that holds for exactly what it has now, as naima verify writes it; holds set by hand without one — naima set, naima new --set — is refused |
| `leaves-development-proved` | a model leaves development (its models item becomes stable, or is created stable) only when at least one property is verified on it and every one holds on a run of exactly what it has now; refused otherwise, naming each property that does not |

**Credits**, printed by `naima credits`

| Name | Version | Licence | Authors |
|---|---|---|---|
| naima-codegen | commit 5aca11dbb1e0 | MIT | the Naima team |

**Landing reports**, checked by `naima land` before a landing (refuses, or blocks until its proofs are current) or printed after it (reports)

| Report | When | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| `properties-current` | blocks | the properties of what the landing changed — their model, a file their last run read, or the property itself — that do not hold on a run of what the branch has now, models in development left out: each one refuses the landing |

**Gates**, listed by `naima gates`

| Gate | Title | What it is for | How it decides | In the full suite |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `properties` | Every property holds | every property holds on a run of what the project has now, outside models in development | blocked by every properties item that is open, violated or in error, or that holds on a run its property, verifier, model, options or input files have changed since; a property of a model in development is owed instead. Part of the full suite a release gate requires; the tool's version is checked by naima check. | yes |

**Verifiers**, used by `naima verify`

| Verifier | What it checks |
|---|---|
| `example-regex` | line-regex properties over a text file: "some <re>" or "never <re>" |
| `naima-codegen` | a naima-codegen project, its codegen.toml the model: "refines" runs check-refinement, that the generated machine stays inside the model; "properties", or one property's .mcf file, runs check-refinement --properties on the refined systems; every file of the project is an input |

## tools

The tools plugins need, installed by Naima into its own directory on the machine it runs on: naima tools reports them, installs one with consent, removes one.

Its contributions' qualified ids are `tools/<name>`.

A plugin declares each tool it needs under `contributes.tools`: an exact version, a licence, its programs, how an install is verified, and per platform a source — url, size, sha256, format — or the answer saying why there is none. `naima tools` reports, for this machine, each declared tool as installed, missing or unavailable. `naima tools install <tool>` prints the plan — the tool and those it needs, each with source, size and licence — and goes on only with consent: a yes on a terminal, or `--consent` with `--by`, recorded in the receipt. It downloads into a staging directory, checks the size and the sha256, unpacks with the platform's own programs (`tar`, `hdiutil`; a `.deb` without dpkg; a `pip` source into a venv, hash-checked), runs the declared check, and renames the install into `<dir>/<tool>/<version>`. The directory is `$NAIMA_TOOLS`, or `~/Library/Application Support/naima/tools` (macOS), `~/.local/share/naima/tools` (Linux), `%LOCALAPPDATA%\naima\tools` (Windows): nothing goes on PATH or into the system, and deleting it removes every tool. A plugin finds an installed program with `installedProgram`. `--host` asks a host the long-work plugin declares, through its own Naima; an install there shows its plan and asks the consent here.

**Extension points** it declares: `tools`.

### naima tools

The tools the loaded plugins declare, on this machine or a declared host: what is installed, missing or unavailable; show what an install would fetch; install one with consent into Naima's own directory, its download checked and the tool verified, never touching PATH or the system; remove one; print an installed program's path.

**Enforces**: An install fetches only the declared source, refuses a size or sha256 that differs, keeps nothing that fails its verification, and goes on only with consent — a yes on a terminal, or --consent with --by, recorded in the receipt; nothing is written outside the tools directory; a tool another installed tool needs is not removed.

**Progress**: Install: the stage download with the bytes received of the declared size, its rate and ETA; then unpack and verify, without a count; with tools it needs, the tools installed of those to install.

```sh
naima tools [--json] [--host <h>]
naima tools show <tool> [--json] [--host <h>]
naima tools install <tool> [--consent "<the yes, restated>" --by <who>] [--host <h>]
naima tools remove <tool> [--host <h>]
naima tools path <tool> [<program>]
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--json` |  | print the report, or the plan, as JSON |
| `--host` |  | ask this host, declared in the long-work plugin's hosts option, through its own Naima over ssh |
| `--consent` |  | the yes of the person whose machine it is, restated: an install without a terminal needs it |
| `--by` |  | who gave the consent: needed with --consent |

Examples:

```sh
naima tools
naima tools show mcrl2
naima tools install mcrl2
naima tools install storm --consent "yes, install Storm" --by owner
naima tools install mcrl2 --host lab
naima tools remove storm
naima tools path storm python
```

## backup

A remote for every repository Naima relies on: the owner is asked once whether to create a private GitHub repository for one that has none.

Its contributions' qualified ids are `backup/<name>`.

A repository with no remote lives on one machine and is lost with it. The repositories Naima relies on are the project's and, when the tracker is kept private beside the code, the tracker's own. For each one with no remote, `naima init`, or the next `naima update` of an existing installation, says the question to ask the owner, once: whether to create a private GitHub repository for it, or keep working locally. On a yes, `naima backup create` uses gh, GitHub's command-line tool: when it is missing, Naima installs it into its own tools folder with the owner's consent, from GitHub's release archive, its checksum verified, without administrator rights; then gh signs in through the browser, showing a one-time code to copy and paste, and creates the private repository and pushes to it. Without a browser, the owner makes an empty private repository at github.com/new and `naima backup add <its address>` adds it and pushes. A no is recorded in that repository's git config (`naima.backup`), and every later `naima hello` says in one line that it is not backed up by a remote. For the project's repository, the owner is also told that GitHub takes no file over 100 MB.

### naima backup

The remote of each repository Naima relies on — the tracker's own, kept private beside the code, and the project's: say which have one; create a private GitHub repository with gh, after the owner's yes; add one the owner made by hand; record that the owner keeps one on this machine.

**Enforces**: A repository Naima relies on is never left without a remote unless the owner said so: the owner is asked once, at init or at the next update, and a no is recorded and recalled by naima hello.

**Progress**: none — gh's sign-in and its repository creation have no progress interface; instead, The install of gh reports its download through naima tools; gh's own lines are shown as it prints them.

```sh
naima backup [create [--repo tracker|project] [--name <name>] [--consent "<yes>" --by <who>] [--no-browser]
naima add <address> [--repo tracker|project]
naima decline [--repo tracker|project]]
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--repo` |  | which repository: tracker (its own repository, kept private beside the code) or project; the one holding the tracker by default |
| `--name` |  | create: the name of the repository on GitHub; the project folder's name by default, with -tracker for the tracker's |
| `--consent` |  | create: the owner's yes, restated, recorded with gh when Naima installs it |
| `--by` |  | create: who said yes |
| `--no-browser` |  | create: say how to make the repository by hand at github.com/new and add it, instead of signing in through a browser |

Examples:

```sh
naima backup
naima backup create --repo tracker --consent "yes, make it private on GitHub" --by owner
naima backup add https://github.com/<owner>/<project>-tracker.git --repo tracker
naima backup decline --repo tracker
```

**Summary sections**: `backup`.

**Setup**, put in place by `naima init` and `naima update` where missing

| Step | What it puts in place |
|---|---|
| `backup-question` | for each repository Naima relies on that has no remote and was never asked about: the question to put to the owner, once, recorded as asked |

**Tools**, installed by `naima tools install`

| Tool | Version | Licence | Platforms |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gh` | 2.103.3 | MIT | darwin-arm64, darwin-x64, linux-x64, linux-arm64, windows-x64 |

## verifier-mcrl2

The mCRL2 adapter: a property is a modal mu-calculus formula over an mCRL2 specification.

Its contributions' qualified ids are `verifier-mcrl2/<name>`.

Off until `naima.json` names it under `plugins`, since it starts programs. Contributes the `mcrl2` verifier and the `mcrl2` tool. `model` is an mCRL2 specification; `property` is a modal mu-calculus formula, inline, or the path of an `.mcf` file from the project root, which is then an input of the run. A property chooses its route in `verifierOptions.route`. `lps`, the default, is the standard route: `mcrl22lps`, `lps2pbes --counter-example`, and `pbessolve` with an evidence file: `true` holds; `false` is violated, and the evidence, printed by `lps2lts` as an `.aut` labelled transition system, is the counterexample; any other answer, or `verifierOptions.timeoutSeconds` reached by a step, is unknown. `lts`, the LTS route, is for a model whose state space is small but whose data makes the standard route slow. `mcrl22lps` and `lps2lts` (with `--threads` from `verifierOptions.threads`) make the LTS once per model version, kept in the run work folder under a key over the model's contents, the toolset's version and the recipe, and shared by every property of that model. `verifierOptions.maxStates` caps the states `lps2lts` may explore (`--max`): a state space larger than the cap makes the run unknown, its output beginning `state cap reached:`, and the LTS cut short is not kept; on the standard route the option is an error, since that route explores with `pbessolve`. Each formula is then reduced only by an equivalence that preserves and reflects it, the coarsest of three: `branching-bisim` for a formula of the fragment the branching equivalences preserve — every visible step right after a star over an action formula that includes tau, no single step that includes tau, fixpoints only as the four inevitability patterns — when it has no fixpoint and no deadlock through a star; `dpbranching-bisim` when it has one of those, which see divergence; `bisim`, strong bisimilarity, for every other formula. With a branching equivalence, `ltsconvert` first hides every action the formula does not mention, unless a label joins such an action to another, in which case the formula takes `bisim` and nothing is hidden. The output says which equivalence was used and why; the reduced LTS is kept beside the LTS, one per equivalence and set of hidden actions, for every formula that needs the same. On the reduced LTS, `lts2pbes --counter-example` and one `pbessolve` with an evidence file decide; on false, the evidence, printed by `ltsconvert` as an `.aut` labelled transition system, is the counterexample, over the reduced LTS, where the hidden actions appear as tau. `cross-check` runs both routes and gives a verdict only when they agree; a disagreement is an error whose output begins `the routes disagree:`. Each run records in its `details` the route, the version of every tool it started, and for the LTS route the LTS's key, reuse and size, the mentioned and hidden actions, the equivalence it reduced by and why, the reduced size and whether it was reused, and on false that the counterexample comes from the reduced LTS. While a step runs, every line it prints is the run's progress: `lps2lts` its states, level and transitions, `pbessolve` its BES equations, `ltsconvert` and `lts2pbes`, started with `--verbose`, their stages. The tools are taken from `bin` when it is given and exists on this machine, otherwise from the mCRL2 202607.0 that `naima tools install mcrl2` installed on this machine, otherwise from PATH; a `bin` that does not exist on this machine, as when a shared `naima.json` names another machine's path, is said once and passed over. The plugin declares that tool, so `naima tools` reports it. A tool that is not there is an error run whose output begins `tool missing:`; a tool that fails is an error with its output. The version recorded is the first line of `mcrl22lps --version`. For `naima equivalent`, it compares two versions of a model modulo `bisim` (strong bisimilarity, the default, which preserves every formula) or `dpbranching-bisim` (divergence-preserving branching bisimilarity, which preserves the formulas the LTS route accepts): `mcrl22lps`, `lps2lts` and `ltsinfo` for each version, the new one through the LTS cache, then `ltscompare --counter-example`; on false, the distinguishing formula it writes is what tells them apart.

Options, each with the default it takes when nothing sets it:

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `bin` | `installed, then PATH` | the absolute directory holding the mCRL2 tools; not given, or not existing on this machine (said once), the mCRL2 naima tools installed on this machine, then PATH |

**Verifiers**, used by `naima verify`

| Verifier | What it checks |
|---|---|
| `mcrl2` | an mCRL2 specification against a modal mu-calculus formula, inline or an .mcf file: by the standard route (mcrl22lps, lps2pbes, pbessolve), by the LTS route (the state space once per model, reduced per formula by the coarsest equivalence that preserves it, lts2pbes, pbessolve), or both, cross-checked; the evidence is the counterexample |

**Tools**, installed by `naima tools install`

| Tool | Version | Licence | Platforms |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mcrl2` | 202607.0 | BSL-1.0 | darwin-arm64, darwin-x64, linux-x64, linux-arm64 (none), windows-x64 |

## ui

The views plugins contribute, a provisional window onto the project, shown in a native window or the browser from a server on this machine only, until the new UI replaces it.

Its contributions' qualified ids are `ui/<name>`.

The provisional window starts a server bound to the loopback interface, on a free port, that refuses every request without the token of its run, and opens it in a native window titled Naima. Each view is one a plugin contributes to `ui-views`, rendered from the files at each request, so the window shows what the files hold now. The first screen holds the views that are panels — the summary, which this plugin renders from every plugin's summary section exactly as `naima summary` does; the gates, from the gates plugin, as `naima gates` reports them; what is next, from the triage plugin, as `naima view next` ranks it; the claims, from the coordination plugin, as `naima claims` recombines them — and every other view is a tab: the boards, which this plugin renders as `naima board` does, one type at a time; the session notes across branches, from the coordination plugin, as `naima pass --list`; one item, which this plugin renders as `naima show` does, its evidence first — its attachments and the items of a type that can prove it, each marked proves, refutes or not yet — and to which every item reference of the window links; the metrics and the others. `/data/<view>` answers the same view's data as JSON, the same data the command prints with `--json`. Closing the window stops the server. The window is a webview, loaded from JSR at a pinned version, only by it, and in a process of its own: the rest of Naima has no dependency. Where it cannot open — on Node or Bun, on a system it does not run on, offline on its first run, when it fetches its library — the default browser opens instead, and it says so in one line.

**Extension points** it declares: `ui-views`.

**UI views**, the tabs of the provisional window

| View | Title | Where | What it shows |
|---|---|---|---|
| `summary` | Summary | first screen | where the project stands: every plugin's summary section, as `naima summary` prints it; its data is `naima summary --json` |
| `board` | Boards | tab | a type's board, its open items by section, most urgent first: `?type=` picks the type (the first one that takes new items), `?all=1` adds the done ones; its data is `naima board <type> [--all] --json` |
| `item` | Item | tab | one item, picked by `?item=`: its evidence — its attachments and the items of a type that can prove, whether each proves or refutes now — then its fields, its other links and its prose; its data is `naima show <item> --json`, null when none is picked |

## metrics

Named measurements — a command's number, a code-quality number taken in process, a test suite's results — recorded per commit, held to a budget, a floor or a baseline, and read back along the commit timeline.

Its contributions' qualified ids are `metrics/<name>`.

A metric is a name and the command that measures it — test time, coverage, lint warnings, size, how long an analysis runs — or a code measure Naima takes itself from the files: lines of code, files, functions, function size, cyclomatic complexity, duplication, TODO markers, dependencies — or a file a benchmark or a profile writes. The project declares its metrics as data in its configuration, from scratch or from a preset (`naima metrics presets`). `naima metrics run` runs them and prints every number with the one it is compared to: the last recorded on an earlier commit of this line of history, and the bound. A bound is a budget (`atMost`), a floor (`atLeast`) or a baseline (`equals`); a `ratchet` makes a gain fail until the bound follows it, so a budget only goes down and a floor only up; loosening a bound names the item that says why. A metric that measures a requirement names it in `satisfies`, and `naima check` notes a requirement that names a time, a memory, a throughput or a size with no such metric. A **test suite** is a test command whose machine-readable report — JUnit XML, TAP, libtest JSON (`test-formats`) — is read per test. Each suite gives three metrics, `<suite>.passed`, `<suite>.failed` (held to none) and `<suite>.seconds`, and `naima metrics run` runs it once for all of them — or, when a recorded run has exactly its inputs, reuses that run and says so; `--force <reason>` runs it again. `--record` writes the numbers, with the commit they measure, as evidence, one file per run, and each suite's run under `test-runs/`: every test's name, result, duration and message, the commit, the inputs' digest, and the log. A test item that names tests in `testNames` gets their result: status passed or failed, the run attached and named in `lastTestRun`, `evidenceKind` observation, and `redSeen` once it passes after a recorded failing run. The `suites` gate holds when every suite passed on HEAD by a recorded run, and names each run. `naima metrics backfill` measures past commits — code measures from git's objects, commands in a temporary worktree — so the timeline starts full. `naima metrics trend`, `history` (text, JSON, CSV) and `plot` (an SVG chart or an HTML report, no dependency) read the records back along the commit timeline, and `naima summary`, `naima board` and `naima queue` show where each metric stands. How a number is read is a kind (`metric-kinds`), a code measure (`code-measures`) or a language's function finder (`code-languages`): any plugin may contribute one. Naima may start the programs the metrics and suites name, and only those: the launcher grants each one.

Options, each with the default it takes when nothing sets it:

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `metrics` | `{}` | `plugins.metrics.options.metrics` in `naima-tracker/naima-data/naima.json`: metric name → { "preset", "run": [program, ...args], "prepare", "kind", "pattern", "field", or "measure" with "language", "include", "exclude", "statistic", "window", or "suite" with "field" (passed, failed, skipped, total, seconds), or "file" (a path from the project root) with "kind"; "unit", "says", "better", one of "atMost" \| "atLeast" \| "equals", "ratchet", "tolerance", "because", "satisfies": [requirements] }. kind defaults to exit for a command, which with no bound must equal 0, and to number for a file. A preset fills in the rest; any key beside it overrides it. |
| `suites` | `{}` | `plugins.metrics.options.suites` in `naima-tracker/naima-data/naima.json`: suite name → { "preset" (deno, node, bun, pytest, cargo), "run": [program, ...args], "prepare", "format" (a test format), "report" (the file its report is written to, from the project root or under {tmp}; without it, the output), "inputs" (the paths or patterns of the files it reads; without it, every file outside the tracker), "says" }. Each gives the metrics <suite>.passed, <suite>.failed and <suite>.seconds. |

**Extension points** it declares: `metric-kinds`, `metrics`, `code-measures`, `code-languages`, `test-formats`, `test-suites`.

### naima metrics

The project's metrics — each a name and the command or code measure that takes it — run, recorded per commit, held to a budget, a floor or a baseline, and read back along the commit timeline as a trend, a table or a chart; every number with the one it is compared to.

**Enforces**: Numbers are recorded with the commit they measure; a ratcheted bound only tightens, and loosening one is refused without --because naming the item that says why.

**Progress**: Run: the metrics taken of those asked, each a stage named by its metric; backfill: the commits measured of those to measure; a metric's own command reports nothing while it runs, so the count moves between metrics.

```sh
naima metrics [list]
naima metrics run [name...] [--record] [--force <reason>]
naima metrics bound <name> <value> [--because <item>]
naima metrics trend <name>
naima metrics history [name...] [--json
naima --csv] [--last <n>]
naima metrics backfill [name...] [--since <ref>] [--last <n>] [--every <n>] [--again]
naima metrics plot [name...] [--out <file>] [--html] [--last <n>] [--title <t>]
naima metrics presets [--json]
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--record` |  | run: write the numbers, with the commit they measure, to metrics/ in the data directory; each suite's run, per test, to test-runs/, its results handed to the test items that name them |
| `--force` |  | run: run the suites again although a recorded run has their inputs, for this reason, which the run records |
| `--because` |  | bound: the item that says why a bound is loosened — a budget raised, a floor lowered; refused without it |
| `--json` |  | history: one JSON list of commits, each with its date and values; presets: a ready declaration of every preset |
| `--csv` |  | history: comma-separated, one row per commit — commit, date, then each metric |
| `--last` |  | history and plot: only the last n commits recorded; backfill: the last n commits of the first-parent line (default 30) |
| `--since` |  | backfill: the commits after this ref, on the first-parent line up to HEAD |
| `--every` |  | backfill: every nth commit, counting back from HEAD, which is always measured |
| `--again` |  | backfill: measure commits already recorded too |
| `--out` |  | plot: write the chart to this file instead of printing it |
| `--html` |  | plot: a page with the chart and a table of where each metric started and where it is now, instead of the bare SVG |
| `--title` |  | plot: the chart's title |

Examples:

```sh
naima metrics
naima metrics run --record
naima metrics run tests coverage
naima metrics run unit --record
naima metrics run unit --force "a flaky failure to confirm"
naima metrics bound test-time 140 --because bugs/slow-ci
naima metrics trend tests
naima metrics history --csv
naima metrics backfill --last 50 --every 5
naima metrics plot coverage complexity --last 50 --out quality.svg
naima metrics plot --html --out quality.html
naima metrics presets
```

**Checks**, run by `naima check`

| Check | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `metric-bound-because` | a metric's `because` names an item of the tracker |
| `test-suites` | a suite's format is a known test format; a test item's testSuite names a declared suite, and its testNames match a test of that suite's last recorded run (a note) |
| `metric-satisfies` | every item a metric's `satisfies` names exists; a metric that satisfies a requirement has a budget, a floor or a baseline (a note) |
| `performance-requirement-has-metric` | a requirement whose title or page names a measure — a time, a memory, a throughput, a size — is satisfied by a metric that measures it, with a budget (a note) |

**Directories** it owns under the tracker root: `metrics/`, `test-runs/`.

**Summary sections**: `metrics`.

**Setup**, put in place by `naima init` and `naima update` where missing

| Step | What it puts in place |
|---|---|
| `code-metrics` | the built-in code-quality metrics that fit the project's languages, with no bounds, declared where plugins.metrics.options has no metrics yet: once, so a project whose owner removed them is not proposed them again |

**UI views**, the tabs of the provisional window

| View | Title | Where | What it shows |
|---|---|---|---|
| `metrics` | Metrics | tab | the project's metrics along the commit timeline: a chart and a table of each, for the metrics and the commits picked |

**Metric kinds**, how `naima metrics` reads a number

| Kind | What it reads |
|---|---|
| `exit` | the command's exit code: 0 is a pass; with no bound it must equal 0 |
| `number` | the first group of `pattern` in the output, stdout then stderr — with no pattern, the first number |
| `count` | how many lines of the output match `pattern` (every non-blank line, with none): warnings, findings, files |
| `duration` | how many seconds the command took, wall clock |
| `json` | the number at `field`, a dotted path, in the JSON the command prints — an array there counts its entries: `deno lint --json`'s diagnostics |

**Code measures**, taken in process by a metric's `measure`

| Measure | Unit | Better | What it measures |
|---|---|---|---|
| `loc` | lines | neither | lines of code: lines with code on them, comments and blank lines left out |
| `files` | files | neither | how many files, of the languages selected |
| `functions` | functions | neither | how many functions, methods and arrow functions, in the languages that find them (TypeScript, JavaScript, Rust) |
| `function-size` | lines | lower | lines per function: a `statistic` of them — mean (default), median, p90, max or sum |
| `complexity` |  | lower | cyclomatic complexity per function, estimated: a `statistic` of it — mean (default), median, p90, max or sum |
| `duplication` | % | lower | the share of code lines inside a run of `window` (default 6) consecutive lines that appears more than once |
| `todos` | markers | lower | how many TODO, FIXME, XXX and HACK markers the files carry — or matches of `pattern` |
| `dependencies` | dependencies | lower | how many dependencies the manifests declare: package.json, deno.json(c) imports, requirements.txt, go.mod, Cargo.toml |

| Language | Files | Functions and complexity |

| `typescript` | .ts .tsx .mts .cts | yes |
| `javascript` | .js .jsx .mjs .cjs | yes |
| `python` | .py |  |
| `rust` | .rs | yes |
| `go` | .go |  |

| Format | What it reads |
|---|---|
| `junit` | JUnit XML, from a file (`report`) or the output: pytest --junit-xml, deno test --reporter=junit, node --test-reporter=junit, bun test --reporter=junit, and most CI tools |
